# 1. Introduction

This project analyzes road accident records, explores factors associated with accident severity, and compares Logistic Regression and Random Forest classification models.

The target variable is `Accident_severity`. The results describe associations in the dataset and do not prove causation.

# 2. Load packages

```{r packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(caret)
library(randomForest)
library(nnet)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(corrplot)
```

# 3. Load the dataset

```{r load-data}
data_path <- if (file.exists("RTA Dataset.csv")) {
  "RTA Dataset.csv"
} else {
  "../RTA Dataset.csv"
}

raw_data <- read.csv(
  data_path,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("", " ", "na", "NA", "N/A", "n/a",
                 "null", "NULL", "None")
)

cat("Dataset dimensions:\n")
print(dim(raw_data))

head(raw_data)
str(raw_data)
summary(raw_data)
```

# 4. Initial data-quality checks

```{r data-quality}
cat("Missing values per column:\n")
print(colSums(is.na(raw_data)))

cat("Total missing values:", sum(is.na(raw_data)), "\n")
cat("Duplicate rows:", sum(duplicated(raw_data)), "\n")
```

# 5. Clean and prepare the data

```{r cleaning}
rta <- raw_data

# Clean text fields and standardize missing-value markers.
for (col in names(rta)) {
  if (is.character(rta[[col]])) {
    rta[[col]] <- trimws(rta[[col]])

    missing_text <- tolower(rta[[col]]) %in%
      c("", "na", "n/a", "null", "none")

    rta[[col]][missing_text] <- NA_character_
  }
}

# Remove duplicate records.
rta <- rta[!duplicated(rta), ]

# Do not invent labels for missing target values.
if (!"Accident_severity" %in% names(rta)) {
  stop("Accident_severity column not found.")
}

rta <- rta[!is.na(rta$Accident_severity), ]

# Convert time into a time-of-day category.
if ("Time" %in% names(rta)) {
  time_text <- as.character(rta$Time)

  parsed_time <- as.POSIXct(
    time_text, format = "%H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC"
  )

  alternative <- is.na(parsed_time) & !is.na(time_text)

  parsed_time[alternative] <- as.POSIXct(
    time_text[alternative], format = "%H:%M", tz = "UTC"
  )

  hour <- suppressWarnings(
    as.integer(format(parsed_time, "%H", tz = "UTC"))
  )

  rta$Time_period <- cut(
    hour,
    breaks = c(-1, 5, 11, 17, 23),
    labels = c("Night", "Morning", "Afternoon", "Evening"),
    include.lowest = TRUE
  )

  rta$Time <- NULL
}

# Remove identifiers and casualty-level fields that may leak
# information about outcomes already observed.
remove_columns <- c(
  "Accident_ID",
  "Casualty_class",
  "Sex_of_casualty",
  "Age_band_of_casualty",
  "Casualty_severity",
  "Work_of_casuality",
  "Fitness_of_casuality"
)

rta <- rta %>% select(-any_of(remove_columns))

# Remove columns that contain no observed values.
all_missing <- names(rta)[
  vapply(rta, function(x) all(is.na(x)), logical(1))
]

all_missing <- setdiff(all_missing, "Accident_severity")

if (length(all_missing) > 0) {
  rta <- rta %>% select(-all_of(all_missing))
}

rta$Accident_severity <- droplevels(
  as.factor(rta$Accident_severity)
)

cat("Cleaned dataset dimensions:\n")
print(dim(rta))

cat("Severity distribution:\n")
print(table(rta$Accident_severity))
```

# 6. Split the data and handle missing values

The split occurs before imputation. Numeric medians and categorical modes are learned from the training set and then applied to the test set.

```{r split-impute}
set.seed(123)

train_index <- createDataPartition(
  rta$Accident_severity,
  p = 0.80,
  list = FALSE
)

train_data <- rta[train_index, , drop = FALSE]
test_data <- rta[-train_index, , drop = FALSE]

target <- "Accident_severity"
predictors <- setdiff(names(train_data), target)

# Remove predictors that are completely missing in training data.
all_missing_train <- predictors[
  vapply(
    train_data[predictors],
    function(x) all(is.na(x)),
    logical(1)
  )
]

if (length(all_missing_train) > 0) {
  train_data <- train_data %>%
    select(-all_of(all_missing_train))

  test_data <- test_data %>%
    select(-all_of(all_missing_train))
}

predictors <- setdiff(names(train_data), target)

get_mode <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x[!is.na(x)])

  if (length(x) == 0) {
    return("Unknown")
  }

  values <- unique(x)
  values[which.max(tabulate(match(x, values)))]
}

# Store preprocessing values for future predictions.
preprocess_info <- list()

for (col in predictors) {

  if (is.numeric(train_data[[col]])) {

    med <- median(train_data[[col]], na.rm = TRUE)

    if (!is.finite(med)) {
      med <- 0
    }

    train_data[[col]][is.na(train_data[[col]])] <- med
    test_data[[col]][is.na(test_data[[col]])] <- med

    preprocess_info[[col]] <- list(
      type = "numeric",
      value = med
    )

  } else {

    train_values <- as.character(train_data[[col]])
    mode_value <- get_mode(train_values)

    train_values[is.na(train_values)] <- mode_value
    train_levels <- unique(train_values)

    test_values <- as.character(test_data[[col]])
    test_values[is.na(test_values)] <- mode_value

    # Replace categories that were not seen during training.
    unseen <- !test_values %in% train_levels

    if (any(unseen)) {
      test_values[unseen] <- mode_value
    }

    train_data[[col]] <- factor(
      train_values,
      levels = train_levels
    )

    test_data[[col]] <- factor(
      test_values,
      levels = train_levels
    )

    preprocess_info[[col]] <- list(
      type = "categorical",
      value = mode_value,
      levels = train_levels
    )
  }
}

train_data$Accident_severity <- droplevels(
  as.factor(train_data$Accident_severity)
)

test_data$Accident_severity <- factor(
  test_data$Accident_severity,
  levels = levels(train_data$Accident_severity)
)

cat("Training rows:", nrow(train_data), "\n")
cat("Testing rows:", nrow(test_data), "\n")
cat("Missing values in training:", sum(is.na(train_data)), "\n")
cat("Missing values in testing:", sum(is.na(test_data)), "\n")
```

# 7. Exploratory data analysis

## 7.1 Accident severity distribution

```{r severity-distribution}
severity_count <- table(rta$Accident_severity)

severity_percentage <- prop.table(severity_count) * 100

severity_summary <- data.frame(
  Severity = names(severity_count),
  Count = as.integer(severity_count),
  Percentage = round(as.numeric(severity_percentage), 2)
)

knitr::kable(severity_summary)

ggplot(rta, aes(x = Accident_severity)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Road Accident Severity",
    x = "Accident severity",
    y = "Number of records"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 7.2 Analyze driver, vehicle, road, weather and lighting factors

```{r factor-analysis, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
analysis_columns <- c(
  "Age_band_of_driver",
  "Driving_experience",
  "Sex_of_driver",
  "Type_of_vehicle",
  "Number_of_vehicles_involved",
  "Road_surface_conditions",
  "Road_allignment",
  "Weather_conditions",
  "Light_conditions",
  "Area_accident_occured",
  "Number_of_casualties",
  "Cause_of_accident"
)

analysis_columns <- intersect(analysis_columns, names(rta))

for (col in analysis_columns) {

  p <- ggplot(
    rta,
    aes(x = .data[[col]], fill = Accident_severity)
  ) +
    geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
    labs(
      title = paste("Accident severity by", col),
      x = col,
      y = "Number of records",
      fill = "Severity"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

  print(p)
}
```

numeric_data <- rta %>% select(where(is.numeric))

if (ncol(numeric_data) >= 2) {

# 8. Train Logistic Regression

```{r logistic-model}
set.seed(123)

logistic_model <- caret::train(
  Accident_severity ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  method = "multinom",
  trControl = trainControl(method = "none"),
  trace = FALSE
)

logistic_model
```

# 9. Train Random Forest

```{r random-forest}
set.seed(123)

rf_model <- randomForest(
  Accident_severity ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  ntree = 300,
  importance = TRUE
)

rf_model
```
```{r balanced-random-forest}
set.seed(123)

# Give fatal injuries more importance
class_weights <- c(
  "Fatal injury" = 5,
  "Serious Injury" = 2,
  "Slight Injury" = 1
)

rf_model_balanced <- randomForest(
  Accident_severity ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  ntree = 300,
  importance = TRUE,
  classwt = class_weights
)

# Evaluate using the same test dataset
balanced_predictions <- predict(
  rf_model_balanced,
  newdata = test_data
)

caret::confusionMatrix(
  balanced_predictions,
  test_data$Accident_severity
)
```



```{r stronger-class-weights}
set.seed(123)

class_weights_strong <- c(
  "Fatal injury" = 20,
  "Serious Injury" = 3,
  "Slight Injury" = 1
)

rf_model_strong <- randomForest(
  Accident_severity ~ .,
  data = train_data,
  ntree = 300,
  importance = TRUE,
  classwt = class_weights_strong
)

strong_predictions <- predict(
  rf_model_strong,
  newdata = test_data
)


strong_cm <- caret::confusionMatrix(
  strong_predictions,
  test_data$Accident_severity
)

print(strong_cm)

```



# 10. Evaluate the models

```{r evaluate-models}
logistic_predictions <- predict(
  logistic_model,
  newdata = test_data
)

rf_predictions <- predict(
  rf_model,
  newdata = test_data
)

logistic_cm <- confusionMatrix(
  logistic_predictions,
  test_data$Accident_severity
)

rf_cm <- confusionMatrix(
  rf_predictions,
  test_data$Accident_severity
)

logistic_cm
rf_cm
```

The weighted models are compared on the same held-out test set. Class weights may improve detection of rare classes, but the resulting predictions must be evaluated for both missed cases and false alarms.
## 10.1 Compare accuracy

```{r model-comparison}
# Recall for a class = correctly predicted cases / all actual cases of that class.
get_class_recall <- function(cm, class_name) {
  tab <- cm$table
  if (!class_name %in% rownames(tab) || !class_name %in% colnames(tab)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  actual_count <- sum(tab[, class_name])
  if (actual_count == 0) return(NA_real_)
  as.numeric(tab[class_name, class_name] / actual_count)
}

model_comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Logistic Regression", "Random Forest", "Weighted Random Forest (20/3/1)"),
  Accuracy = c(
    as.numeric(logistic_cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
    as.numeric(rf_cm$overall["Accuracy"]),
    as.numeric(strong_cm$overall["Accuracy"])
  ),
  Fatal_Injury_Recall = c(
    get_class_recall(logistic_cm, "Fatal injury"),
    get_class_recall(rf_cm, "Fatal injury"),
    get_class_recall(strong_cm, "Fatal injury")
  ),
  Serious_Injury_Recall = c(
    get_class_recall(logistic_cm, "Serious Injury"),
    get_class_recall(rf_cm, "Serious Injury"),
    get_class_recall(strong_cm, "Serious Injury")
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  transform(
    model_comparison,
    Accuracy = round(Accuracy, 4),
    Fatal_Injury_Recall = round(Fatal_Injury_Recall, 4),
    Serious_Injury_Recall = round(Serious_Injury_Recall, 4)
  ),
  caption = "Comparison on the held-out test set"
)

ggplot(model_comparison, aes(x = Model, y = Accuracy)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Model Accuracy Comparison",
    x = "Model",
    y = "Accuracy"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 15, hjust = 1))
```

## 10.2 Class-wise metrics

```{r class-metrics}
cat("Logistic Regression class-wise results:\n")
print(logistic_cm$byClass)

cat("\nRandom Forest class-wise results:\n")
print(rf_cm$byClass)

cat("\nWeighted Random Forest class-wise results:\n")
print(strong_cm$byClass)
```


```{r confusion-matrix-plot}
# Create a visual confusion matrix for Random Forest
cm_table <- as.data.frame(rf_cm$table)

ggplot(cm_table, aes(x = Reference, y = Prediction, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = Freq), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest Confusion Matrix",
    x = "Actual Accident Severity",
    y = "Predicted Accident Severity",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
```

Since fatal accidents may be uncommon, inspect the fatal class's precision and recall rather than relying on overall accuracy alone.

# 11. Random Forest feature importance

```{r importance}
importance(rf_model)

varImpPlot(
  rf_model,
  main = "Random Forest Variable Importance"
)
```

Feature importance indicates which variables the model relies on; it does not establish causation.

# 12. Results summary

```{r results-summary}
print(model_comparison)

best_accuracy_model <- model_comparison$Model[
  which.max(model_comparison$Accuracy)
]
cat("Highest-accuracy model:", best_accuracy_model, "\n")
cat("Important: model selection should also consider fatal- and serious-injury recall, not accuracy alone.\n")
```

# 13. Prepare and save the model for the Shiny app

The app uses five driver and environmental inputs. This compact model is saved with the training factor levels so the app can construct compatible inputs.

```{r five-feature-model}
# Select the five inputs for our prediction app
selected_columns <- c(
  "Age_band_of_driver",
  "Driving_experience",
  "Weather_conditions",
  "Road_surface_conditions",
  "Light_conditions"
)

# Train a model using only these five inputs
set.seed(123)

rf_model_five <- randomForest(
  x = train_data[, selected_columns, drop = FALSE],
  y = train_data$Accident_severity,
  ntree = 100,
  importance = TRUE
)

# Test the model
five_feature_predictions <- predict(
  rf_model_five,
  newdata = test_data[, selected_columns, drop = FALSE]
)

print(
  caret::confusionMatrix(
    five_feature_predictions,
    test_data$Accident_severity
  )
)

# Save the model so app.R can use it
saveRDS(
  list(
    model = rf_model_five,
    train_data = train_data,
    selected_columns = selected_columns
  ),
  file = "road_accident_model_bundle.rds"
)

cat("Model saved successfully!")
```


# 14. Conclusion

This project examines accident severity patterns, performs data preparation, and compares Logistic Regression with Random Forest using a held-out test set.

Use the actual metrics and charts generated by the report to describe your findings. Do not claim that any factor causes accident severity based on these observational data.
